desc:
A rooted tree on nodes 1 to n is a directed graph in which exactly one node (the root) has no incoming edge, every other node has exactly one incoming edge (from its parent), and every node can be reached from the root by following edges.

You are given edges, where edges[i] = [u, v] is a directed edge from u to v. The list is a rooted tree on n nodes to which one extra directed edge was added (so it has exactly n edges).

Return an edge that can be removed so that the remaining n - 1 edges form a rooted tree. If several edges work, return the one that appears last in the input.

edges = [[1,2],[1,3],[2,3]]       result = [2,3]
edges = [[2,1],[3,1],[4,2],[1,4]] result = [2,1]
edges = [[1,2],[2,3],[3,1]]       result = [3,1]
constraints: 1 ≤ u, v ≤ n and u ≠ v
The edges are a rooted tree plus exactly one extra edge
hints: After adding one edge there are only two ways it can break the tree: some node gets two parents, or a cycle appears (sometimes both).

If some node v has two incoming edges, one of those two must go. Call the earlier one first and the later one second. Try ignoring second and run union-find on the rest: if it still makes a cycle, first must be the culprit.

If no node has two parents, the extra edge points at the root and closes a cycle. Run union-find over the edges in order (ignoring direction); the edge that first joins two nodes already connected is the last edge of the cycle in input order, which is the answer.
editorial: Count the parents of each node. Case 1: a node v has two incoming edges first and second (in input order). The answer is one of these two, since removing anything else leaves v with two parents. Rebuild the graph without second and run union-find on the remaining edges (ignoring direction). If a cycle shows up, then second was not the problem and first must be removed; otherwise removing second already gives a valid tree and, as the later edge, it is the answer to return.

Case 2: every node has at most one parent. Then the extra edge points at the root, and the whole graph is one cycle with trees hanging off it. Union-find over the edges in order finds the first edge whose endpoints are already connected; that edge is the last edge of the cycle in input order, and removing any cycle edge gives a valid rooted tree, so the last one is the answer.
Time is O(n · α(n)) and space O(n). The tricky part is not the data structure but the case analysis: handle the two-parents case first, then fall back to the pure-cycle case.
